items.title: Synthetic Data Generation in the Era of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey
items.abstract: Background: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has dramatically advanced the capabilities of Natural Language Processing (NLP), enabling breakthroughs in text understanding, generation, and reasoning. However, the success of these models hinges on access to massive, diverse, and high-quality labeled datasets. In many real-world scenarios, such as specialized domains (e.g., healthcare, law), low-resource languages, and privacy-sensitive applications, curating such data remains prohibitively expensive, time-consuming, or infeasible due to regulatory or ethical constraints. Moreover, as LLMs continue to scale in size and complexity, the demand for training and evaluation data grows disproportionately, exacerbating annotation bottlenecks and domain coverage gaps. Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to address these challenges by programmatically producing task-specific or domain-adapted examples that complement or replace manually labeled data. Initially grounded in statistical modeling and deep generative architectures, SDG has evolved into a central strategy for improving data efficiency, mitigating distributional shifts, and enabling scalable supervision in modern NLP pipelines, especially in conjunction with LLM-driven prompt-based learning and self-supervised generation. Objectives: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of SDG techniques up to November 2026, with a particular focus on LLM-oriented pipelines. We categorize generative approaches for synthetic text, identify trends in controllability, verification and automation, and highlight open challenges in evaluation, fairness, privacy and scalability. Methods: We review the model families used to generate synthetic text, including probabilistic models, autoencoders and variational autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), transformers, diffusion language models and mixtures of experts, as background for LLM-based pipelines such as instruction synthesis, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), prompt evolution, feedback loops and multi-agent generation, together with toolkits such as PromptSource [1], Self-Instruct [2] and LM-Debugger [3]. The original literature was collected informally; we extended it with a documented search run on 14 November 2026 (49 queries, 78 candidate records, 47 works added) covering 2025–2026 work on reasoning traces and verifiable rewards, model collapse and data quality, agentic and multi-agent pipelines, and evaluation, privacy and multilingual generation. The scope is text and language data, with other data types only where an LLM generates or directs their generation, and every reference was checked against arXiv, Crossref or the publisher. Results: Our synthesis traces an evolution from static, single-model pipelines to modular, verifier-centred and agentic systems in which LLMs plan, generate, critique and check data. Since 2025, synthetic data has become central to teaching models to reason: verifiable rewards move the bottleneck from preference labels to problems with checkable answers, which procedural generators, rephrased web text and self-play now supply. Studies of model collapse show that accumulating real and synthetic data avoids collapse while replacing real data does not, but also that even small synthetic fractions and recursive training can degrade models and their fairness. Synthetic text can leak membership information about its source data, and differentially private generation methods are narrowing the utility gap. Evaluation practice remains fragmented, and multilingual generation increasingly relies on culturally grounded rather than translated data. Conclusions: LLM-driven SDG is rapidly transforming data creation, making it more scalable, controllable and adaptive, but its reliability now depends on verification, provenance and privacy safeguards. This survey offers a taxonomy and a roadmap for building trustworthy synthetic data systems, and it motivates future work on verifiers beyond checkable domains, standardized evaluation of data generators, collapse-aware data practice and formal privacy guarantees.

items.title: Teacher–GenAI partnership in design and technology education: From utility to allyship
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping Design and Technology (D&T) education by transforming how design ideas are generated, evaluated, and refined. Although existing research has largely focused on capabilities and limitations of AI, less is known about the emerging teacher–GenAI relationships during authentic design practice. Through semi-structured and recall interviews, classroom observations, reflective journals, design folios and artefacts, this qualitative case study investigated these relationships. Guided by sociomaterial perspectives and using reflexive thematic analysis, the study examined how creativity, agency, knowledge construction, pedagogy, and ethical decision-making emerged through human–GenAI interaction. Findings revealed that pre-service teacher–GenAI partnerships evolved through a developmental trajectory from utility, to dialogue, to teacher orchestration, and ultimately allyship. Rather than functioning as a solution-generating tool, GenAI became a provocateur and generative partner whose educational value emerged through iterative cycles of prompting, critique, reflection, and redesign. The study proposes Orchestrated Co-Agency and the Teacher–GenAI Relationship Continuum as complementary conceptual lenses for understanding these interactions. These lenses could offer new theoretical insights into human–AI co-creation and inform curriculum, pedagogy, and the responsible integration of GenAI in Design and Technology education.

items.title: Teaching and assessing reflective writing in generative AI-mediated higher education: Vignettes and provocations
items.abstract: This Pecha Kucha presentation offers a situated account of teaching and assessing in the evolving context of generative AI-mediated higher education. It aims to open up space for contemplation and dialogue around the complexities of the current teaching and learning landscape, where students and educators alike are grappling with new norms, and much grace and understanding needs to be extended on both sides as each learns from, and with, the other how to better navigate the complex nuances and permutations of AI-mediated academic work. Drawing on experiences from a postgraduate academic writing course that I teach, I share a selection of pedagogical vignettes and provocations emerging from my marking of the end-of-semester reflection assignments for the course. This assignment, requiring students to highlight key insights gained from the course and to reflect on these with reference to course discussions and their own scholarly practices, is one that I have greatly enjoyed marking over the years. However, vastly different patterns of engagement have been emerging from the students in recent semesters, and it seems evident that the affordances of generative AI, in changing how students tackle academic assignments, are at the same time disrupting some of higher education’s long-held assumptions about what constitutes learning, writing, and ownership. The pedagogical encounters highlighted include: students asking my own course chatbot to reflect on the course for them, reflections being flagged by AI-detection software as being potentially entirely AI-generated, diverse understandings regarding what constitutes one’s “own work” where AI has been used to assist in the writing process, and students unquestioningly accepting AI’s reformulations as “better” than their own (even when they were not). Encountering these has caused frustration, but I also see in these examples deeper epistemological and pedagogical tensions. Literacy scholars, particularly those working within an “Academic Literacies” perspective (e.g. Jones et al., 1999; Lea & Street, 1998; Lillis, 2003), have long argued that reading and writing are “social practices.” They are, in other words, situated within, influencing and being influenced by, the social and cultural contexts in which they take place. The educational landscape of today, with its myriad AI-assisted possibilities, raises questions of whether, how, and to what extent, our conceptions about “learning,” “writing,” and “ownership” may need recalibration. In fact, scholars have begun to recognise that current writing practices resulting in hybrid texts co-constructed by humans and AI are making it difficult, if not impossible, to identify distinct boundaries between AI-generated output and a student’s own intellectual efforts (e.g. Eaton, 2023; Wu et al., 2026). Higher education is in a season where excitement, curiosity, and unease about generative AI’s impact on academic work and learning sit in tension. Even as one who has actively sought to engage students in discussions of how we can productively and legitimately use generative AI in our writing, I found myself having unexpected reactions (of relief) when I encountered assignments with linguistic infelicities of the sort that suggested their writers had not used generative AI. The way forward, this presentation suggests, requires an intentional commitment to prioritise pedagogical approaches that foreground human connection – both in terms of cultivating a renewed intellectual and emotional connection of students with their own work, and in terms of building connection between students and instructors through open dialogue and compassionate, nuanced approaches to teaching and assessing.

items.title: Teaching beyond AI: Gamified problem-based formative assessment aligned with UNESCO AI competency frameworks
items.abstract: The arrival of capable generative AI (GenAI) tools has posed a genuine and largely unresolved challenge for summative assessment in higher education. When AI-generated submissions evade institutional detection 94% of the time and examination scores rise sharply without any change in teaching, the evidentiary basis of take-home and invigilated assessment is genuinely in question. This paper draws on two lines of work to argue that classroom-based gamified problem-based formative assessment (GPBFA) offers a more durable response than detection-focused approaches. The first line is an empirical study of saval.app, a GPBFA platform evaluated through Keller’s ARCS motivational model across a full university semester (pre n = 41, post n = 44). Results across all four ARCS dimensions were encouraging (all p < .0001; Cronbach’s alpha > .93; composite 81% positive response rate), with near-zero motivational decline across 12 weeks. The second line is a review of UNESCO’s 2024 AI Competency Frameworks for Teachers and Students, which we argue are philosophically and pedagogically aligned with classroom GPBFA in ways the existing literature has not yet made explicit. Taken together, we suggest that moving assessment into the classroom — where it is live, observed, and problem-centred — may address both the integrity challenge and the AI literacy imperative that UNESCO frameworks define.

items.title: TempQuant: Learning Adaptive Temperatures for Quantized Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.

items.title: THE APPLICATION OF GAMIFICATION IN LITERATURE EDUCATION: IMPROVING STUDENTS' MOTIVATION AND ENGAGEMENT
items.abstract: This article examines the application of gamification in literature education as a means of increasing students' motivation and engagement. It analyses the theoretical foundations of gamification, including self-determination theory and game-based learning principles, and describes a quasi-experimental study in which game elements such as points, levels, badges, quests and narrative roles were integrated into literature lessons. The findings indicate that a carefully designed gamified environment strengthens intrinsic motivation, encourages regular reading, improves participation in discussions and deepens students' interpretation of literary texts.

items.title: The apprenticeship layer: What assessment reform cannot secure on its own
items.abstract: Australian higher education has responded to generative artificial intelligence with an ambitious program of assessment reform. Structural approaches, most visibly the two-lane model, seek to sustain trust in degrees by securing some assessments while opening others to AI partnership. This conceptual paper argues that the reform consensus, now sharpened by sector attention to assurance of learning and adaptive capabilities, addresses validity more directly than formation. Assessment tasks are not only measurement occasions; they can also be sites of the cognitive work through which capability develops. Drawing on cognitive apprenticeship, desirable difficulties and cognitive offloading, the paper introduces the apprenticeship layer: the stratum of entry-level cognitive work through which expertise has historically been developed and renewed. As AI is increasingly used to perform parts of this work in workplaces and universities, institutions face a risk of certifying capabilities without reliably preserving the practice through which those capabilities are formed. The paper proposes three principles for formation-centred design: friction by design, process as both learning and evidence, and a care floor of guaranteed human attention. It concludes that valid judgement and capability formation are different questions that assessment can and should be designed to answer together.
